text: Two weeks after the last lesson's VM went live, Briarcliff Systems spins up a second Linux VM in the same subnet, and a ticket lands on your desk: can't SSH into the new VM, the connection just hangs. Nothing about this is exotic — it's one of the most common early-career cloud tickets there is. What matters is the order you check things in.

Before touching networking at all, you confirm the VM's power state is actually running, which rules out the simplest explanation. Next you check whether the network security group's rule really allows port 22 from where you're connecting. Then the route table, to rule out a bad custom route overriding the normal path. Only after all of that do you check sshd and its logs on the VM itself.

Listing the NSG rules turns up the likely culprit: the inbound SSH rule still allows traffic only from 203.0.113.0 slash 24, the range Briarcliff's office used when this subnet was first set up. But the team moved offices last month, and their outbound IP now falls in a completely different range, 198.51.100.0 slash 24. The rule never changed; the office did. Traffic from the new office never matches it, so the security group silently drops it — no error, just a hang.

A quick check of the route table shows the default path to the internet is untouched, so that's ruled out too. And on the VM itself, reached through the serial console, systemctl status sshd shows the service active, while auth.log is essentially empty — no attempts at all, which means the traffic genuinely never arrived. The fix is a one-line update to the NSG rule's source range, and the SSH connection succeeds immediately.

Notice the order: confirm the VM is running, check the cloud configuration wrapped around it — the security group and the route table — and only then check the operating system and its services. That's broadest and fastest first, narrowest last, and it's exactly how this course's chapters stack, from packets and addressing up through the cloud networking constructs that wrap around a running Linux host.

That same habit — network layer, then cloud configuration, then OS and services — is exactly what the next course in this path builds on directly. Course complete: next up, Microsoft Azure Administration, Compute & Storage, where this same layered instinct goes to work inside one cloud platform in real depth.
